newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila insists rebels accept its sovereignty.
newsitem.headline: Manila insists rebels accept its sovereignty.

text.p: The Philippines said on Thursday that any peace agreement with communist rebels must be based on the guerrillas' acceptance of its sovereignty.

Peace talks between government and rebel negotiators were suspended earlier this week after disputes between the two sides over how to implement any agreements they might reach on ending the 28-year Marxist insurgency.
The talks are being hosted by the Netherlands where most of the leaders of the local communist party live in self-exile.

Negotiators of the communist-led National Democratic Front (NDF) have accused the government panel of derailing the talks by demanding that all agreements between them must be in line with Philippine constitutional and legal processes.
This is tantamount to "demanding the capitulation" of the NDF, chief rebel consultant Jose Maria Sison said in a statement on Thursday from the Netherlands, faxed to news organisations in Manila.
Chief government negotiator Howard Dee said his panel was only "defending the sovereignty of the state."
"Philippine sovereignty is one and indivisible and does not allow for two governments, two constitutions and two rules of law," Dee said in a statement.
Manila has previously rejected an NDF demand for a so-called "status of belligerency," which officials said was equivalent to giving the rebels recognition as a virtual government.
The two sides earlier agreed to speed up their negotiations so that an agreement could be reached by the end of June.
More than 40,000 people have died in the rebellion since it began in 1969.

Manila says rebel armed strength, which peaked at about 26,000 fighters in the late l980s, has dwindled to some 5,000 as a result of the collapse of communism in Europe, dissension among rebel leaders and the surrender of many of their followers.
